title: Mas v. Perry (1974)
summary: The spouses’ temporary Louisiana residence did not destroy diversity from their Louisiana landlord.
notes:
The syllabus abbreviates this case as “Perry.” Search by Mas or Perry reaches this record. The separate A.F.A. Tours entry addresses the course’s principal amount analysis.

Jean Paul Mas (French citizen) and Judy Mas (Mississippi domiciliary) sued their Baton Rouge landlord for invasion of privacy; the jury awarded $5,000 to Mr. Mas and $15,000 to Mrs. Mas. Perry also argued Mr. Mas's $5,000 award fell short of the jurisdictional amount, and the Fifth Circuit rejected that because the claim exceeding the amount was made in good faith.

sections.Parties: The Mas spouses, graduate students, sued Perry, their Louisiana landlord. The husband was a French citizen and the wife had been domiciled in Mississippi.
sections.Material Facts: The plaintiffs discovered that the landlord had observed them through two-way mirrors in their rented residence. They lived in Louisiana while pursuing graduate study. The record did not show that the wife had changed her Mississippi domicile by forming the required intention to remain in Louisiana. Marriage to a French citizen did not automatically give her his citizenship for this purpose. The jury awarded different amounts to the spouses, but the assigned excerpt focuses on citizenship.
sections.Procedural History: The plaintiffs brought a federal diversity action and obtained a verdict. Perry contested the jurisdictional basis. The court of appeals sustained jurisdiction under its analysis of the parties’ citizenship.
sections.Issue: Did the wife’s Louisiana residence as a student or her marriage to a French citizen eliminate the diverse citizenship required for the suit?
sections.Holding: No. Her Mississippi domicile continued on the record, and the husband’s French citizenship supplied his separate jurisdictional position.
sections.Reasoning: Residence and citizenship are not interchangeable. Domicile includes physical presence together with the relevant intention to remain; an existing domicile persists until a new one is established. The temporary educational setting and the absence of the necessary intent prevented treating the wife as a Louisiana citizen merely because she lived there. Each spouse’s citizenship required its own analysis. The decision therefore resists substituting a mailing address or family status for the jurisdictional inquiry.

learning.why: The spouses’ temporary Louisiana residence did not destroy diversity from their Louisiana landlord.

topics.cp-citizenship: A person’s domicile requires more than temporary residence.
topics.cp-diversity: The spouses’ citizenship had to be determined separately.
topics.cp-domicile: The wife’s student residence in Louisiana did not establish an intention to remain there indefinitely.
topics.cp-amount-in-controversy: The Fifth Circuit also held that Mr. Mas's $5,000 verdict did not defeat jurisdiction because the amount claimed in good faith controls.
topics.cp-usc-1332: The case applies 1332's complete-diversity and alienage provisions to a French husband and a Mississippi wife.
